label: Lecture 11: How It Is Asked
rows: Name the rhythm
Rhythm naming is fair game: strips appear with the vignette. Read every strip the same five ways.
Values come with ranges
Any rate or interval in a stem carries its normal range (rate 60–100 per minute).
★ The atrial rule
“If there is P waves, the rhythm is atrial. Remember that, that's very important.”
Not now (said out loud)
The U wave (“Don't focus on that right now”), the word hexaxial, and all treatment (“That'll be next week”).

label: Conduction System & Pacemakers
rows: Sinoatrial node
Main pacemaker, upper right atrial wall below the superior vena cava. 60–100 per minute.
Atrioventricular node
Near the coronary sinus. BACKUP pacemaker, 40–60 per minute. Zones: transition, compact, trigger.
Purkinje network
Third pacemaker (both nodes failed), 20–40 per minute. Conducts FASTEST of all.
Bachmann's bundle
Right atrium to left atrium: the main interatrial route.
Internodal tracts
Superior anterior (FAST), middle, inferior posterior (SLOW). In most people only the fast tract truly reaches the node.
Bundle of His
The ONLY path atria → ventricles in a normal heart (the atrioventricular septum does not conduct).
Bundle branches
Left splits into THREE fascicles: posterior, septal (septum = Q wave), anterior. Right is MUCH LONGER.
Passive filling
70–80% of ventricular filling needs no atrial contraction.

label: Cardiac Cell & Action Potential
rows: Four properties
AUTOMATICITY (own impulse) · EXCITABILITY (responds) · CONTRACTILITY · CONDUCTIVITY (cell to cell). The pacemaker hierarchy keeps lower cells quiet.
Phase order
Phase 4 / 0
4 = rest, −90 millivolts, potassium inside. 0 = upstroke: fast SODIUM rushes in.
Phase 1 / 2 / 3
1 = the notch. 2 = plateau: CALCIUM in → contraction. 3 = repolarization: calcium closes, POTASSIUM OUT, back to −90 (slides say potassium “in”; truth and the slide 17 figure say out).
Absolute refractory
No response at all; about 180 milliseconds; QRS start to the T wave PEAK.
Relative refractory
Responds, but fragile; T wave peak to end. The T wave peak divides the two.
Vector
Left and down, toward the front. Lead II looks straight along it: the rhythm lead.

label: Paper, Waves & Intervals
rows: Paper
25 millimeters per second. Small box 0.04 SECONDS, 1 millimeter (slide says “0.04ms”). Large box 0.2 seconds, 5 millimeters. Horizontal = time, vertical = voltage. Calibration 10 millimeters tall.
P wave
Atrial depolarization. Round, upright in lead II, ≤2.5 millimeters, under 0.12 seconds.
★ PR interval
P onset to QRS start. 0.12–0.20 seconds (3–5 small boxes), constant. Blocks, accessory pathways, alternate pacemakers move it.
★ QRS
Ventricular depolarization; a complex of Q, R, S. Under 0.12 seconds; 0.12 or more = abnormal ventricular conduction.
Q / R / S

Q = septum (away from lead II), under 0.04 seconds. R = ventricular depolarization toward lead II (deck: anterior left ventricle). S = away from lead II (deck: lateral wall); must cross baseline, else “S wave pattern”.
J point / ST / T
J = QRS meets ST, at baseline ±1 millimeter. ST = ventricles holding contraction. T = ventricular repolarization, asymmetric.
QT
QRS start to T end; all ventricular activity. 350–450 milliseconds males, 360–460 females. QTc: Lecture 7 (no slide here).
TP segment
Resting state; the BEST isoelectric reference (not the PR segment).

label: Leads
rows: Bipolar I, II, III
Einthoven's triangle. Lead II: POSITIVE LEFT FOOT, negative right shoulder. Lead I: left shoulder +, right shoulder −. Lead III: left foot +, left shoulder −.
Unipolar augmented
aVR, aVL, aVF (augmented vector right, left, foot): one physical lead + a theoretical central terminal (the deck says Wilson's; strictly that is the chest leads' reference).
Chest leads
Unipolar, HORIZONTAL view. V1 4th space right of sternum · V2 4th left · V3 between · V4 5th midclavicular · V5 anterior axillary · V6 midaxillary.
Who looks where
V1–V2 septal · V3–V4 anterior · I, aVL, V5, V6 lateral · II, III, aVF inferior. Contiguous = same area.

label: Rate, Regularity & the Five Steps
rows: ★ Six-second method
QRS count × 10 = ventricular rate; P waves × 10 = atrial rate. The most used; works on irregular rhythms.
Count-down
Heavy lines from an R wave: 300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50. Unreliable below 50.
300 ÷ large boxes; 1500 ÷ small boxes between R waves. 1500 is the MOST ACCURATE.
Regularity
Compare consecutive R to R intervals; calipers (or marked paper) if unsure.
★ Five steps
Rate → regularity → P waves → PR interval → QRS. Every strip, every time.
Married P waves
Each P wave is causing its QRS. A P before every QRS = atrial origin; uniform upright P = sinus node.

label: The Sinus Rhythms
rows: Normal sinus rhythm
60–100, regular, normal married P waves, PR 0.12–0.20 constant, narrow QRS.
Bradycardia / tachycardia
Same criteria; rate under 60 / over 100. QRS narrow or wide. RATE is the only difference.
Sinus arrhythmia
60–100, IRREGULAR, otherwise sinus. Benign, most common in children. Inspiration → vagal tone suppressed → rate UP; exhalation → down.
Sinus exit block
Node fires, impulse BLOCKED: whole cycle missing (no P, QRS, T). P to P MARCHES OUT (gap = multiple of the cycle).
Sinus pause
Node STOPS and restarts; cycle RESETS; does NOT march out.
Sinus arrest
Like a pause but AT LEAST THREE cycles missed; resets.
Sick sinus syndrome
Exit block + pause + arrest in one patient (even one strip). Rare.
